claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the ability to develop a mechanically stable, passivating oxide film along grain boundaries.
A passivating grain-boundary oxide film limits corrosion damage.
A mechanically stable grain-boundary oxide film distributes mechanical stresses during wear.
The film's corrosion protection and stress distribution synergistically reduce wear and corrosion.
The initial alloy has a uniform, random solid-solution microstructure.
The initial alloy has minimal pre-existing passivating grain-boundary films.
Controlled oxidation or heat treatment can promote passivating oxide-film formation at grain boundaries.
The proposed intervention produces grain boundaries decorated by a thin, mechanically stable passivating oxide film.
The grain-boundary film acts as a barrier to corrosive attack.
The grain-boundary film lowers localized degradation by distributing mechanical stresses during wear.
Without the film, chemical erosion accelerates at wear-damaged sites because fresh reactive surfaces are continuously exposed.
Samples with enhanced grain-boundary passivation will have a lower overall degradation rate under combined wear and corrosion than conventionally processed controls.
Enhanced grain-boundary passivation will reduce wear depth or material volume loss.
Enhanced grain-boundary passivation will reduce the corrosion rate.
Combined degradation in passivated samples will be less severe than the sum of independently measured wear and corrosion effects.
The prediction holds when corrosive and mechanical loads are moderate enough for the film to remain intact.
Extreme wear can overwhelm the film's mechanical integrity and cause the proposed mechanism to fail.
The mechanism can fail when environmental chemical aggressiveness exceeds the film's protective capability.
